card.profile: Pettathullal is a historic ritualistic dance performed annually during the Mandalam-Makaravilakku pilgrimage season at Erumely in Kottayam district, Kerala. Executed primarily by devotees—including first-time Sabarimala pilgrims known as Kanni Ayyappas—the ritual celebrates the victory of Lord Ayyappa over the demoness Mahishi. Dancers paint their faces and bodies with vibrant colours and charcoal, carry wooden weapons, and move in rhythmic step to traditional percussion ensembles. Moving from the Petta Sree Dharmasastha temple around the neighbouring Vavar mosque and onward to the Valiyambalam Sastha temple, the performance is a striking expression of communal harmony and religious devotion.

card.profile_long:
Pettathullal is an annual ritualistic dance performed in the town of Erumely in the Kottayam district of Kerala, India. Rooted in the sacred traditions of the Sabarimala pilgrimage during the Mandalam-Makaravilakku season spanning November to January, the dance reenacts the ecstatic joy of the local populace following the victory of Lord Ayyappa over the demoness Mahishi. The main event takes place on the 27th day of the Malayalam month of Dhanu. Participation is spearheaded by two main traditional regional groups: the Ambalappuzha group and the Alangadu group. The Ambalappuzha team begins their preparatory journey days earlier on the 22nd of Dhanu, visiting the Manimala Bhagavathy temple on the 25th of Dhanu to perform an Aazhi pooja before arriving for the main ceremony.

Before the physical dance begins, participants undertake solemn rituals of atonement known as Prayashchitham. Devotees offer a coin and a betel leaf on their sacred travel kit, the irumudikettu, to seek forgiveness for intentional and unintentional sins committed during their period of strict vows and fasting (vrata kalam). Following this, pilgrims offer Pettapanam kettal or Dakshina to the senior leader, the Periyaswami. First-time pilgrims to Sabarimala, known as Kanni Ayyappas, carry a bundle filled with vegetables and cereals suspended on a stick rested across their shoulders. As part of their mandatory ritual initiation, these first-time devotees must carry a wooden arrow (sarakkol) throughout the entire dance performance.

To begin the dance, participants dress in tribal attire, smearing their faces and torsos with brilliant colours and black charcoal. Grasping wooden maces and arrows, they form groups and initiate the dance at the Petta Sree Dharmasastha temple (Kochambalam). The performance features energetic rhythmic stepping, jump-like movements, and continuous vocal chanting of the sacred refrain "Ayyappa thinthakathom, Swamy thinthakathom." Instrumental accompaniment is provided by powerful traditional ensembles playing Chenda melam, Nagaswaram, and Pambamelam, alongside chanted mantras and devotional hymns.

A central feature of Pettathullal is its deep connection to interfaith unity. The dance procession moves directly from the Kochambalam temple to the adjacent Vavar mosque, dedicated to Lord Ayyappa's Muslim companion, Vavar. At the mosque, the pilgrims are warmly welcomed by members of the Mahallu Jamaat committee. After circumambulating the mosque in dance, a representative of Vavar joins and accompanies the procession as it dances another half-kilometer to the Valiyambalam Sastha temple. The ritual is performed in two distinct temporal segments: the Ambalappuzha group dances in the morning after observing a sacred eagle (Krishna parunth) circling in the sky, believed to be Lord Vishnu on Garuda, while the Alangadu group dances in the afternoon, awaiting the appearance of a sacred star in the daytime sky before sunset.
card.sacred_note: Pettathullal is a sacred pilgrimage ritual connected to Lord Ayyappa and the Sabarimala pilgrimage. Outsiders should respect all religious observances, dietary/fasting vows (vrata kalam), and local temple customs. Participation in the ritual steps and carrying of sacred items (such as the irumudikettu and sarakkol) is traditionally reserved for practicing devotees.

sections.origins_and_history: Pettathullal is a historic ritualistic tradition associated with the Sabarimala pilgrimage at Erumely in Kottayam district, Kerala. The dance commemorates the joyful celebration of the local people following the mythological destruction of the demoness Mahishi by Lord Ayyappa. Historically, the ritual involves two distinct communities: the Ambalappuzha group and the Alangadu group. The Ambalappuzha group starts their journey on the 22nd of Dhanu, visiting the Manimala Bhagavathy temple on the 25th of Dhanu for an Aazhi pooja prior to the main event on the 27th of Dhanu. Traditional belief holds that Lord Vishnu travels from the Ambalappuzha Sree Krishna temple riding Garuda—manifested as a Krishna parunth (sacred eagle) flying overhead—to witness the ritual.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is executed in group formations by pilgrims who chant "Ayyappa thinthakathom, Swamy thinthakathom" in rhythm with loud percussion ensembles. Dancers leap and step rhythmically while holding wooden weapons such as sarakkol (arrows) and wooden maces. First-time Sabarimala pilgrims (Kanni Ayyappas) carry a bundle filled with cereals and vegetables tied to a stick across their shoulders, alongside a mandatory wooden arrow. The movement starts at the Kochambalam temple, circles the Vavar mosque, and proceeds 0.5 km to the Valiyambalam Sastha temple.
sections.music_and_instruments: The ritual dance is accompanied by vibrant traditional instrumental ensembles, sacred mantras, and vocal hymns. Key instruments specified in the traditional performance include Chenda melam (percussion ensemble), Nagaswaram (double-reed wind instrument), and Pambamelam (traditional drumming). The dancers themselves contribute to the acoustic environment by continuously chanting the rhythmic refrain "Ayyappa thinthakathom, Swamy thinthakathom".
sections.costume_and_setting: Participants dress in tribal-style attire, smearing their faces and bodies with bright paints and charcoal. They carry symbolic wooden weapons including sarakkol (arrows) and wooden maces. Kanni Ayyappas also carry a shoulder stick with a tied bundle containing vegetables and grains. The physical setting spans three primary sacred sites in Erumely: beginning at the Petta Sree Dharmasastha temple (Kochambalam), passing around the adjacent Vavar mosque, and concluding at the Valiyambalam Sastha temple located 0.5 km away.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Pettathullal is celebrated annually on the 27th day of the Malayalam month of Dhanu during the Mandalam-Makaravilakku pilgrimage period (spanning November, December, and January). The ritual signifies spiritual purification and the victory of good over evil as represented by Ayyappa's defeat of Mahishi. It begins with 'Prayashchitham' (atonement for sins committed during the fasting period) through offerings of betel leaves and coins on the irumudikettu travel kit, followed by offering Dakshina (Pettapanam kettal) to the Periyaswami. The event also stands as a famous symbol of Hindu-Muslim communal harmony due to the integration of the Vavar mosque into the sacred procession.
sections.notable_figures: The performance involves key traditional roles rather than individual artistic performers. These include the Periyaswami (the chief elder/leader who receives Dakshina), the Kanni Ayyappas (first-time pilgrims who must perform specific rituals with wooden arrows), members of the Ambalappuzha and Alangadu traditional groups, and representatives of the Mahallu Jamaat committee of the Vavar mosque who welcome the dancers.
sections.regional_variants: Two distinct traditional groups perform regional variations of the ritual on the same day: the Ambalappuzha group and the Alangadu group. The Ambalappuzha group performs earlier in the day following the sighting of the sacred eagle (Krishna parunth) in the sky. The Alangadu group performs their thullal in the afternoon, awaiting the appearance of a visible star in the sky prior to sunset before completing their procession around the temple.
sections.lineage: The ritual lineage is preserved through hereditary regional participation by the Ambalappuzha and Alangadu communities, passed down through generations of Sabarimala devotees and led by senior spiritual leaders known as Periyaswamis.
